segments.voice: Two cousins walk into the same bedroom, a few moments apart. Krishna is asleep in his palace at Dwaraka. Duryodhana arrives first and takes a fine seat at the head of the bed. Arjuna comes in after him and stands at the foot of the bed, hands folded. Both have come for the same thing: Krishna's help in the war that now looks likely. Both wait. Krishna wakes, and the first person his eyes fall on is Arjuna.
screen: `TWO COUSINS, ONE ERRAND.` → `THE HEAD OF THE BED, THE FOOT.` → `WHO IS SEEN FIRST?`

segments.voice: Udyoga is a Sanskrit word for effort, for getting ready, and this book of the epic is all preparation: for peace, if it can be found, and for war, if it can't. It started in Virata's hall, where the families talked it through. Balarama, Krishna's brother, said the Pandavas should ask gently, since Yudhishthira had chosen to play that game. Satyaki answered him hotly. King Drupada said: send an envoy, and gather allies too. So both sides go looking for friends, and both end up at Krishna's bed. Krishna makes them an offer. On one side, a huge army of his own fighting men. On the other, Krishna himself, alone, and he will not take up a weapon in the fight. Arjuna may choose first, he says: he saw him first, and he's the younger. Arjuna doesn't hesitate. He chooses Krishna, unarmed. Duryodhana is delighted. He gets the army, and leaves thinking he's won the better half. Now think about what each cousin was really asking for. Duryodhana wanted strength he could count. Arjuna wanted the person. And look back at the bedroom. Duryodhana sat at the head, where a guest of rank sits. Arjuna stood at the feet, the way you stand before someone you honor. Nobody in the story says the seat decided it. The story just shows where each man chose to be, and whose face Krishna saw when he opened his eyes.

segments.voice: Fold your hands, the way Arjuna stands at the foot of the bed, and bring to mind something you're asking for these days, from a person or from life. Breathing in, name it plainly; breathing out, ask underneath it whether this is strength you can count or a presence you want near, and let the question rest with your folded hands, since there's no wrong answer. If you pray, you can bring the asking into your prayer.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-FOURTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Udyoga, the getting ready, began at Krishna's bedside, and Arjuna chose Krishna over an army. Your line was whose face Krishna saw when he opened his eyes.
screen: `UDYOGA.` · `ARJUNA CHOOSES KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: An envoy rides into the Pandava camp. It's Sanjaya, the trusted charioteer and counselor of the blind king Dhritarashtra. He greets everyone warmly, asks after their health, and then delivers his master's message. It isn't an offer. It isn't a threat. It's a plea: don't fight. And something is missing from it. Dhritarashtra asks for peace, but he doesn't offer to give back what was taken.
screen: `SANJAYA RIDES IN.` → `THE MESSAGE: DON'T FIGHT.` → `WHAT THE MESSAGE LEAVES OUT.`

segments.voice: Sanjaya speaks movingly, and the Pandavas don't brush it aside. A war between cousins, he says, means killing your own teachers, your own uncles, your own kin. What kind of victory is that? Better, he says, to live on alms than to win a kingdom that way. Yudhishthira's answer is not angry. I want peace too, he says. Who would choose war if peace were possible? But peace has to mean something. Give us back our own kingdom, Indraprastha, the city we built. Krishna speaks as well. Holding back from action, he says, is no answer by itself; a person must act, and act rightly. In Krishna's reply, Sanjaya's advice sounds holy but asks only one side to give anything up. And then, in this same exchange, Yudhishthira makes a request so small it's almost painful to hear. Not the whole kingdom. Not even the city. Give us five villages, he says, and let this end. Five villages, from men who once ruled. Sanjaya carries the message home. Stay with the shape of the exchange. One side talks about peace as the absence of fighting. The other talks about peace as fairness, and will accept very little of it.

segments.voice: Krishna decides to go to Hastinapura himself: one more try for peace, in person. Before he leaves, each of the brothers gives him a message, and several of them lean toward peace. Then Draupadi comes to him. She takes her long dark hair in her hand, the hair Duhshasana dragged her by in the dice hall, and holds it up. When you speak of peace, she says, remember this. If my husbands won't fight, my old father will, and my sons will. Krishna promises her she'll see justice, and sets off.
screen: `KRISHNA GOES HIMSELF.` → `DRAUPADI HOLDS UP HER HAIR.` → `REMEMBER THIS.`

segments.voice: Hastinapura gets ready for him. Duryodhana has rest houses built along the road and lays out a great feast. This is diplomacy as hospitality: if Krishna eats at his table, he's half won. Krishna passes the rest houses by. In the city he greets the old king, then goes to Kunti, the Pandavas' mother, who has been living in Vidura's house all these years. She weeps and asks after her sons, one by one. Only then does Krishna go to Duryodhana's palace. He accepts his greeting, and declines the meal. Duryodhana is offended. Why won't you eat with us? Krishna's answer is short and sharp. A person eats another's food either out of love, or out of need. You feel no love for me, and I'm in no need. So he walks back to a much plainer house: the home of Vidura, the wise half-brother of the king, who spoke up for the Pandavas years ago in the dice hall. That's where Krishna eats, and where he stays. Look at what he does before he says a word in the assembly. Draupadi's hair goes with him. He won't eat at the table of a man who means harm. He sleeps under the roof of a man who told the truth when it was dangerous. He visits the mother first. An embassy isn't only speeches. It's where you eat, where you sleep, and whom you visit first.

segments.voice: Morning in the great hall of the Kurus. Every seat is filled: Dhritarashtra on his throne, Bhishma, Drona, Vidura, Duryodhana and his brothers, Karna beside them. Krishna walks in, and the hall goes quiet. This is the moment the whole Udyoga has been building toward: a formal chance to stop the war, spoken face to face, in front of everyone who matters.
screen: `THE HALL IS FULL.` → `KRISHNA WALKS IN.` → `A CHANCE TO STOP THE WAR.`

segments.voice: Krishna speaks to Dhritarashtra first, and his argument is simple. You can stop this. Your sons and your nephews could stand together, and no one could stand against them. Peace would be your gain, not your loss. Give the Pandavas their share. Others speak after him. Old sages tell stories of pride brought low. Bhishma and Drona urge Duryodhana to make peace. Duryodhana hears them, and refuses. He says, in effect, that he won't give the Pandavas even as much land as the point of a needle would cover, and he walks out of the hall. Then Gandhari, his mother, is sent for. He is called back to hear her, and she tells her son plainly that a person who can't rule his own anger and greed can't rule a kingdom. He leaves again. Outside, he and his friends make a plan: seize Krishna, tie him up, and the Pandavas will be helpless. Word reaches the hall. And Krishna laughs. The text says that as he laughed, his body blazed, and gods and heroes seemed to stream out of him, so bright the court had to shut their eyes. Only a few could look: Bhishma, Drona, Vidura and the sages, and Dhritarashtra, granted sight for that moment. Then the vision ends, and Krishna walks calmly out. The point isn't only the wonder. Krishna came anyway. The night before, at Vidura's, he said he had come so that no one could blame him for not trying. So he made the whole case for peace in public, where no one could say it was never offered.

segments.voice: A chariot rolls out through the gates of Hastinapura. The embassy has failed. Duryodhana won't give the Pandavas their share, and war is coming. But before Krishna goes, he does something odd. He calls Karna, Duryodhana's friend and champion, up beside him, and the two ride out of the city together, away from the crowd. What Krishna says on that ride could stop the war before it starts, and it rests on a secret about who Karna's mother is.
screen: `THE EMBASSY HAS FAILED.` → `KRISHNA CALLS KARNA UP` → `A SECRET ON THE ROAD`

segments.voice: Here is the secret. Karna is Kunti's son, born to her before she married Pandu. That makes him, Krishna says, the eldest brother of the five Pandavas. Then comes the offer. Come with me. Your brothers will touch your feet. You will be king, and Yudhishthira himself will stand behind your throne. Everything Karna has been denied, the rank, the family, the respect, is laid at his feet in one ride. Karna's answer is the heart of today. He says he already knows. Then he says why it changes nothing. His mother set him adrift as a newborn. A charioteer named Adhiratha found him, and Adhiratha's wife Radha raised him. Her milk fed him and her love kept him alive, he says, and he will not stop being her son for a crown. He married among the charioteer's people, and he has children there. And for years Duryodhana has stood by him when no one else would. He gave Duryodhana his word, and he means to keep it. Then he asks Krishna for one thing: don't tell Yudhishthira. If Yudhishthira learned that Karna was his elder brother, he would hand him the kingdom, and Karna would hand it straight to Duryodhana. Better that it stays secret. So a man is offered everything he ever wanted, and turns it down for the people who loved him first. Some readers hear loyalty in that. Some hear tragedy. The epic lets you hear both.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-EIGHTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday Krishna offered Karna a throne, and Karna chose the mother who raised him. Your line: her milk fed him, her love kept him alive.
screen: `KRISHNA'S OFFER.` · `KARNA STAYS RADHA'S SON.`

segments.voice: On the bank of the Ganga, a man stands facing east with his hands raised, reciting his prayers. The sun climbs and burns the back of his neck, and he doesn't move. Behind him, a woman has come quietly and stands in the shade of his own upper cloth, waiting until he's finished. It's Kunti, and the man is Karna. Yesterday, Krishna asked Karna to change sides. Today, his mother comes to ask the same thing, in person.
screen: `PRAYERS ON THE GANGA BANK` → `KUNTI WAITS IN HIS SHADOW` → `A MOTHER'S REQUEST`

segments.voice: Karna finishes, turns, and greets her by naming himself: I am Karna, son of Radha and Adhiratha. What can I do for you? Hear the sting in that, even if he doesn't intend one. Kunti tells him the truth. You are not a charioteer's son. You are mine, and the Sun's. Come to your brothers. In the text, a voice even speaks from the sun to confirm her words. Karna doesn't doubt her. But his answer is hard to hear. You cast me away when I was born. You never gave me a mother's care. Now, on the eve of war, you come to me for the sake of your other sons. And then, after the hardest words, Karna gives her something. He won't join the Pandavas, but he makes a promise. In the battle he will not kill four of her sons, Yudhishthira, Bhima, Nakula and Sahadeva, even when he has them at his mercy. Only Arjuna will he fight to the end. Either way, he says, you will still have five sons: with Arjuna, or with me. Kunti trembles and embraces him, asks him to remember his promise, and they part. The Udyoga book is the book of getting ready, and both sides use it to gather allies. Karna uses it to give away his advantage, out of love for a mother who gave him up. It's a gift, and it may cost him his life.
screen: `I AM KARNA, SON OF RADHA` · `YOU ARE MINE, AND THE SUN'S` · `FOUR BROTHERS SPARED, NOT ARJUNA` · then, large: `YOU WILL STILL HAVE FIVE SONS`

segments.voice: Think of someone you love where the truth between you is hard. Breathing in, name the hard thing silently; breathing out, name one thing you could still give, even if you can't give everything, and rest between the two, the way Karna did on the riverbank. If you pray, you can bring that person into your prayer.
Udyoga. The book of getting ready. Our days with it end here, on choices made by a river, before the armies take the field.
screen: `UDYOGA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: you will still have five sons. He couldn't give her everything, so he gave her what he could. See you tomorrow.

819.title: Bhishma Parva (the Gita re-read in place, 6 sessions)
819.hook: a blind king is offered sight to watch the war his sons are fighting, and he says no.
819.carry: a listener who chose to hear rather than see
819.tomorrow: Bhishma Parva (the Gita re-read in place, 6 sessions)
819.howItsDone: The Bhagavad Gita is printed and recited on its own, and it is also read in place as part of the Bhishma Parva, where Sanjaya narrates it to the blind king Dhritarashtra.

screen: `DAY EIGHT-HUNDRED-NINETEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday the Udyoga days ended by the Ganga, with Karna's promise to Kunti: four of her sons spared. Your line: you will still have five sons.
screen: `KARNA'S PROMISE.` · `FIVE SONS EITHER WAY.`

segments.voice: The armies are drawn up on the field of Kurukshetra. In the palace at Hastinapura, the blind king Dhritarashtra sits and waits. Then the sage Vyasa comes to him with an offer. If you want to see the battle, he says, I'll give you sight. And the king says no. He doesn't want to see his own family killed. He only wants to hear about it. So Vyasa gives the gift to someone else: Sanjaya, the king's charioteer and counselor. Today the Bhishma book opens, and the Bhagavad Gita, which we've read before, comes back inside the story that holds it.
screen: `THE ARMIES ON KURUKSHETRA` → `THE BLIND KING REFUSES SIGHT` → `SANJAYA WILL SEE FOR HIM`

segments.voice: Earlier on the path we read the Gita verse by verse, as a teaching on its own. For these six sessions, we put it back where it lives: in the middle of a war report. And the frame is stranger than it first seems. After Vyasa's visit, the book doesn't go straight to the first morning of battle. Instead, Sanjaya comes back to the palace with terrible news. Bhishma, the grandsire of the whole family, has fallen. Days of fighting have already passed. Dhritarashtra breaks down, and then asks Sanjaya to tell him everything, from the start. So when the Gita opens with the old king asking what his sons and Pandu's sons did on the field of dharma, he is asking about something already over, the way someone asks after a funeral: tell me how it happened. Every word Krishna says to Arjuna, about duty, about the self that is never killed, about acting without clinging to the result, reaches us through Sanjaya, spoken to a grieving father who refused to look. That changes how the Gita sounds. It's not a lecture in a quiet hall. It's a conversation reported in a dark room, after the worst news, to a listener who chose to hear rather than see. Over the next five sessions: the chariot, the teaching, the vision, and the morning after, all in place.
screen: `THE GITA PUT BACK IN THE STORY` · `THE TELLING STARTS AFTER BHISHMA FALLS` · `A FATHER ASKS: HOW DID IT HAPPEN?` · then, large: `THE GITA, TOLD BY SANJAYA`

segments.voice: Close your eyes, or let them rest on the floor, and be a listener for a moment, not a watcher. Find the nearest sound, then something farther, then the farthest thing you can hear, and simply receive them, the way the king received the whole war through one voice. If you pray, let one sound become the start of your prayer.
Bhishma Parva. The Book of Bhishma, the book of the Mahabharata that holds the Bhagavad Gita inside it. This week carried us from the Udyoga embassy, through Karna's two refusals, to this dark room.
